title: I Stopped Holding My Students Accountable And Here Is What Happened d-heres-what-happened/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin recounts a personal experiment: for one week, midway through a semester with a well-behaved class, he deliberately stopped enforcing his classroom management plan while keeping his personality and demeanor unchanged. As minor misbehavior went unaddressed, he found his relationship with students deteriorating within days—students grew less friendly, made less eye contact, and were slower to follow directions, even though nothing ever became outright disrespectful. By the end of the week he felt his influence and leadership presence fading despite ramped-up friendliness, while several students began anxiously asking if something was wrong with him. On Friday he revealed the experiment, and normal order returned almost immediately once accountability resumed. He concludes that kindness and good humor alone are not enough to sustain a class—students need firm accountability as a counterbalance—and that the experiment gave students a memorable lesson in the value of boundaries.
points: A week-long experiment removing consequences, while keeping demeanor unchanged, caused measurable deterioration in student relationships.
Students grew less friendly and slower to follow directions within days, even without new instances of overt disrespect.
Several students grew anxious and began asking the teacher if something was wrong, sensing the shift in structure.
Kindness and good humor alone proved insufficient to sustain a well-behaved class without accountability as a counterpart.
Restoring the classroom management plan brought order back almost immediately, reinforcing that consequences protect rather than harm the student-teacher relationship.
quotes: For one week, I decided to no longer rely on my classroom management plan. That's right. I just stopped following it.
By Wednesday morning, it was clear that their opinion of me had dropped a few notches.
My leverage and influence was fading before my eyes and my leadership presence was fading before theirs.

One thing I found especially interesting about the experiment, and heartening, frankly, was that as the week went on more and more students approached me to ask variations of, “What are you doing?” “Why are you doing this?” and “Are you okay?
Done right, as we recommend here at SCM, accountability is a powerful force for good. It’s a wonderful benefit for students and indispensable to creating a happy and well-behaved class.
